diagrams.name: spec-p221-diabetes
diagrams.title: Diabetes mellitus: healthy vs Type 1 vs Type 2

labels.answer: Cells fail to respond to circulating insulin

cloze.text: Type 1 diabetes is caused by {{c1::autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic beta cells}}, so no insulin is produced.
Type 2 diabetes is caused by {{c1::insulin resistance}} or reduced insulin output.
Type 1 diabetes has a {{c1::sudden}} onset, usually in {{c2::childhood or adolescence}}.
Type 2 diabetes has a {{c1::gradual}} onset, usually in {{c2::adults}} (but rising in younger people).
Body type: Type 1 diabetics are usually {{c1::thin or normal weight}}; Type 2 diabetics are usually {{c2::overweight or obese}}.
Insulin is {{c1::always}} required in Type 1 diabetes; Type 2 may be managed with {{c2::oral meds, lifestyle changes}}, or insulin.
Classic diabetes symptoms: {{c1::polyuria}} (frequent urination), {{c2::polydipsia}} (excess thirst), {{c3::polyphagia}} (excess hunger), plus weight loss and fatigue.
cloze.extra: Type 2 has the same symptoms, but they are often milder or unnoticed for years.

cloze.text: In Type 1 diabetes there is a risk of {{c1::diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)}}: the body burns fat → acidic ketones, {{c2::fruity breath}}, coma.
cloze.extra: In Type 2, DKA is rare but possible in advanced cases.

cloze.text: Long-term complications of diabetes (both types) include damage to the {{c1::eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart}}.
Diabetes medication can cause {{c1::hypoglycemia}} — keep a {{c2::glucose source}} ready at dental visits.
Diabetes (both types) carries a high risk of {{c1::periodontal disease}} and oral infections such as {{c2::candidiasis}}.
Other oral findings in diabetes: {{c1::xerostomia}}, {{c2::delayed healing}}, {{c3::burning mouth}} and taste changes.
Schedule diabetic patients for {{c1::short, morning}} visits.
The {{c1::oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)}} measures blood sugar {{c2::2 hours}} after drinking a sugary drink; 200 mg/dL or more = diabetes.
An A1C below {{c1::5.7%}} is normal.
An A1C of 5.7%–6.4% indicates {{c1::prediabetes}}.
An A1C of {{c1::6.5%}} or higher = diabetes diagnosis.
cloze.extra: Don't be confused! 6.5%+ means the patient already HAS diabetes — the 7% target is for keeping blood sugar under control once diabetes is confirmed, not for diagnosis.

cloze.text: For most diabetic patients the A1C target (well-controlled diabetes) is {{c1::below 7%}} — individual targets may vary.
cloze.extra: A1C <7% means blood sugar is well controlled, reducing complications including periodontal disease.

cloze.text: AAP perio classification: diabetes affects {{c1::grading}} — A1C <7% = {{c2::Grade B}}, A1C ≥7% = {{c3::Grade C}} (faster disease progression).
The {{c1::thyroid gland}} controls metabolism by producing the hormones {{c2::T3 and T4}}, which regulate how fast the body uses energy, how warm we feel and how fast the heart beats.
In {{c1::hypothyroidism}} ('slow') not enough T3/T4 is produced, slowing body functions; in {{c2::hyperthyroidism}} ('fast') too much is produced, speeding up metabolism.
Common causes of hypothyroidism: {{c1::Hashimoto's}} (autoimmune) and {{c2::iodine deficiency}}.
The common cause of hyperthyroidism is {{c1::Graves' disease}} (autoimmune overstimulation).
Temperature: hypothyroidism → {{c1::cold}} intolerance; hyperthyroidism → {{c2::heat}} intolerance.
Heart rate: hypothyroidism → {{c1::bradycardia}} (slow); hyperthyroidism → {{c2::tachycardia}} (fast).
Weight: hypothyroidism → weight {{c1::gain}} with {{c2::decreased}} appetite; hyperthyroidism → weight loss with increased appetite.
Oral findings in hypothyroidism: {{c1::macroglossia}} (enlarged tongue), dry mouth (xerostomia), {{c2::delayed eruption}} of teeth, malocclusion and an underdeveloped jaw.
Oral findings in hyperthyroidism: {{c1::burning tongue}}, {{c2::early eruption}} of teeth (in children) and stress sensitivity.
Dental implications of hypothyroidism: monitor for {{c1::dry mouth}}, cold sensitivity and {{c2::delayed healing}}.
Dental implications of hyperthyroidism: use stress reduction, {{c1::limit epinephrine}} and monitor for {{c2::cardiac symptoms}}.
{{c1::Graves' disease}} is an autoimmune condition that causes hyperthyroidism; its hallmark sign is {{c2::exophthalmos}} (bulging eyes), plus goiter, insomnia and high anxiety.
The adrenal glands sit {{c1::on top of each kidney}}.
cloze.extra: They produce key hormones that regulate stress response, blood pressure, metabolism and fluid balance.

cloze.text: The adrenal {{c1::cortex}} is the outer layer of the adrenal gland; the adrenal {{c2::medulla}} is the inner part.
The adrenal cortex makes {{c1::cortisol}} (stress hormone) and {{c2::aldosterone}} (controls salt and water balance).
The adrenal medulla makes {{c1::epinephrine and norepinephrine}}, which increase heart rate and blood flow during stress ('fight or flight').
Cortisol helps the body manage stress, regulate {{c1::metabolism}} and maintain {{c2::blood pressure}}.
Constant stress keeps cortisol high, which can shrink the {{c1::hippocampus}} — the part of the brain that controls memory.
cloze.extra: Did you know? Short bursts of stress help you stay alert before an exam; constant worry backfires.

cloze.text: Addison's disease = {{c1::hypocortisolism}}; Cushing's syndrome = {{c2::hypercortisolism}}.
Addison's disease is caused by destruction of the {{c1::adrenal cortex}} → too little {{c2::cortisol and aldosterone}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Addison's = "Need to ADD cortisol" — low energy, low BP → everything is down.

cloze.text: Cushing's syndrome is excess cortisol, often due to a {{c1::tumor}} or {{c2::long-term steroid use}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Cushing's = "Cushy cushion" — weight gain, moon face, buffalo hump (fat at the back of the neck).

cloze.text: Main symptoms of Addison's disease: fatigue, {{c1::low BP}}, poor stress tolerance and skin/oral {{c2::pigmentation}}.
Main symptoms of Cushing's syndrome: weight gain, {{c1::moon face}}, {{c2::buffalo hump}}, high BP and poor healing.
The oral finding of Addison's disease is {{c1::brown/bronze pigmentation}} of the buccal mucosa and gingiva.
Oral findings of Cushing's syndrome: early tooth loss, early eruption, large mandible, {{c1::osteoporosis of alveolar bone}}, periodontal breakdown and delayed healing.
In Addison's disease, stress can trigger an {{c1::adrenal crisis}} — a life-threatening emergency.
cloze.extra: Cushing's: no crisis, but an exaggerated stress response and poor wound healing.

cloze.text: In Addison's disease the body struggles with {{c1::stress}}, {{c2::salt balance}} and blood pressure because it lacks cortisol and aldosterone.
In Cushing's syndrome too much cortisol leads to weight gain, {{c1::fragile tissues}} and poor healing.
The {{c1::pituitary gland}} ('master gland') sits at the {{c2::base of the brain}} and controls many other glands.
The pituitary releases {{c1::growth hormone (GH)}}, {{c2::thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)}} and others that regulate growth, metabolism and reproduction.
Growth hormone affects height, bone size and soft tissues like the {{c1::jaw and tongue}}.
Pituitary dwarfism: {{c1::↓ growth hormone}}, occurs in {{c2::childhood}}; short stature with normal proportions.
Gigantism: ↑ growth hormone {{c1::before}} the growth plates close (childhood); excessive height, long limbs.
Acromegaly: ↑ growth hormone {{c1::after}} the growth plates close ({{c2::adulthood}}); bone thickening in face, hands, feet; joint pain.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Acromegaly = "Adult = After plates close." Pituitary dwarfism and gigantism occur in childhood.

cloze.text: Oral findings of pituitary dwarfism: {{c1::delayed eruption}}, small jaws, crowded teeth.
Oral findings of gigantism: {{c1::enlarged jaws}}, spacing, delayed eruption.
Oral findings of acromegaly: {{c1::macroglossia}}, large mandible, spacing and {{c2::TMJ}} issues.
Hepatitis is {{c1::liver inflammation}} caused by a virus; the types most relevant for dentistry are Hepatitis A, B, C and D.
Hepatitis {{c1::E}} (HEV) spreads through contaminated water like Hep A, but is rare in North America.
Hepatitis A is transmitted by the {{c1::fecal–oral}} route (contaminated food/water).
Hepatitis B is transmitted through blood, {{c1::saliva}}, sexual fluids and {{c2::perinatally}}.
Hepatitis C is transmitted {{c1::bloodborne}} (needles, transfusions).
Hepatitis D is bloodborne and occurs {{c1::only in people with Hep B}}.
Onset: Hep A is {{c1::acute only}}; Hep B is acute or chronic; Hep C is {{c2::often chronic}}; Hep D is chronic (more severe than HBV alone).
Vaccines exist for Hepatitis {{c1::A and B}}; there is no vaccine for Hep C or Hep D — but Hep D is {{c2::prevented by the HBV vaccine}}.
cloze.extra: Healthcare professionals need the Hep B vaccine.

cloze.text: Chronic infection risk: Hep A {{c1::none}}; Hep B moderate; Hep C {{c2::high}}; Hep D high (co-infection worsens liver damage).
Oral (saliva) transmission risk is {{c1::moderate}} for Hep B (saliva, gingival fluid), minimal for Hep A and very low for Hep C and Hep D.
Tuberculosis is a chronic bacterial infection caused by {{c1::Mycobacterium tuberculosis}} that mainly affects the {{c2::lungs}}.
TB spreads by {{c1::inhalation of airborne droplets}} from a cough, sneeze or speech of an infected person.
TB symptoms: {{c1::persistent cough}}, {{c2::night sweats}}, fever, fatigue and weight loss.
Oral findings in TB are rare but may include {{c1::painful ulcers}} on the tongue or palate.
Before elective treatment, ask about a history of TB and confirm {{c1::medical clearance}}.
If a patient with TB is actively contagious, use an {{c1::N95 mask}} and {{c2::postpone non-urgent care}}.
Do not use {{c1::ultrasonic scalers or high-speed handpieces}} if a patient's TB status is unclear.
Notify {{c1::public health authorities}} if undiagnosed active TB is suspected.
HIV attacks and destroys {{c1::CD4 T-cells}} (a type of white blood cell), weakening the immune system.
A normal CD4 count is {{c1::500–1,600}}/mm³.
{{c1::AIDS}} is the final stage of HIV; death usually results from {{c2::opportunistic infections}}.
HIV spreads through {{c1::blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk}} — not through saliva or casual contact.
HIV may be asymptomatic for years; later stages show fever, weight loss, fatigue, night sweats and {{c1::swollen lymph nodes}}.
{{c1::Antiretroviral therapy (ART)}} prolongs life and reduces HIV transmission.
The most common oral finding in HIV is {{c1::candidiasis}}.
In HIV, {{c1::linear gingival erythema}} appears as a red band at the gingival margin.
In HIV, {{c1::hairy leukoplakia}} appears as a white patch on the tongue border.
In HIV, {{c1::Kaposi's sarcoma}} appears as red/purple lesions, often on the palate.
Other HIV oral findings: {{c1::NUG/NUP}} and persistent herpes (widespread, long-lasting).
Treat HIV patients with {{c1::standard precautions}}.
In HIV patients monitor for oral signs of {{c1::immunosuppression}} (e.g., thrush, unexplained ulcers); they may require antifungals or antibiotics for opportunistic infections.
In HIV, avoid elective care during acute illness or {{c1::uncontrolled viral load}}.
Primary syphilis appears about {{c1::3 weeks}} after exposure as a {{c2::painless chancre}} at the infection site (orally: on lips/tongue).
Secondary syphilis appears about {{c1::6 weeks}} after the chancre heals: skin rash, fever, malaise and {{c2::mucous patches}} on the oral mucosa.
Latent syphilis: early = {{c1::<1 year}} after infection, late = >1 year; no symptoms, but still infected.
cloze.extra: Contagious? Early latent = possibly; late latent = no.

cloze.text: Tertiary syphilis occurs years after an untreated latent stage: organ damage (brain, heart, nerves) and {{c1::gummas}}; orally a gumma on the palate or tongue → possible {{c2::perforation}}.
Syphilis is contagious in the {{c1::primary and secondary}} stages, possibly in early latent, and not in late latent or tertiary.
Syphilis cases are rising worldwide — nearly {{c1::tripling}} in the past decade in the U.S. and Canada, including young adults.
cloze.extra: Oral lesions (especially in secondary syphilis) can appear on the tongue, lips or palate and may look like other conditions.

cloze.text: HSV-1 (oral herpes) typically affects the {{c1::mouth, lips and face}}; HSV-2 the {{c2::genital region}}.
Primary HSV-1 infection = {{c1::primary herpetic gingivostomatitis}}: fever, malaise, painful red gums, ulcers on tongue/lips; mostly in {{c2::children}}.
cloze.extra: Primary HSV-2 is often asymptomatic or a mild flu-like illness.

cloze.text: Recurrent HSV-1 = {{c1::recurrent herpes labialis}} (cold sores): tingling → lip sore in the same location.
cloze.extra: Recurrent HSV-2: genital sores triggered by illness or stress.

cloze.text: Recurrent herpes labialis is triggered by stress, {{c1::sunlight}}, trauma and {{c2::dental care}}.
HSV-1 lies latent in the {{c1::trigeminal ganglion}}; HSV-2 in the {{c2::sacral ganglion}}.
HSV-1 is transmitted by {{c1::saliva}}, kissing, shared utensils and aerosol contact; HSV-2 by sexual contact.
HSV-1 is highly contagious during both primary and {{c1::recurrent}} outbreaks — {{c2::delay elective care}} if active.
cloze.extra: HSV-2 is contagious even without visible sores.

cloze.text: Healing time of HSV-1: primary {{c1::10–14 days}}; recurrent {{c2::7–10 days}}. (HSV-2: 2–3 weeks.)
HSV-1 in the dental setting carries a very high risk of {{c1::herpetic whitlow}}, eye infection and aerosol transmission — use PPE and reschedule non-urgent care during active outbreaks.
cloze.extra: HSV-2 dental relevance is low unless cross-infection occurs via oral–genital contact.

cloze.text: Herpes is treated with {{c1::acyclovir}} or valacyclovir (especially early in the outbreak), plus palliative care for discomfort.
About 8% of human DNA comes from ancient viruses called {{c1::endogenous retroviruses (ERVs)}}.
cloze.extra: Did you know? They inserted genetic material into reproductive cells and became part of the human genome; they helped shape pregnancy and the immune system.

cloze.text: {{c1::End-stage renal disease (ESRD)}} is the final stage of chronic kidney disease: the kidneys can no longer filter waste, leading to a buildup of toxins ({{c2::uremia}}).
Healthy kidneys filter waste, balance electrolytes, regulate blood pressure and activate {{c1::vitamin D}}.
In {{c1::hemodialysis}}, the patient's blood is removed, filtered by a machine outside the body and returned clean — like a mechanical kidney.
ESRD is most often caused by {{c1::diabetes}}, {{c2::hypertension}} or long-term kidney damage.
Signs/symptoms of ESRD: fatigue, nausea, weakness, {{c1::pale skin}} and {{c2::high blood pressure}}.
ESRD requires {{c1::dialysis}} (usually 2–3×/week for 3–5 hours) or a {{c2::kidney transplant}} to survive.
Schedule dental visits for a dialysis patient {{c1::the day after dialysis}}, when the patient is more stable and bleeding is less likely.
Oral signs to monitor in ESRD: {{c1::uremic breath}}, {{c2::metallic taste}}, xerostomia, candidiasis, stomatitis and bleeding gingiva.
{{c1::Cyclosporine}} (Sandimmune), an anti-rejection drug for transplant patients, can cause {{c2::gingival hyperplasia}}.
The kidneys filter about {{c1::50 gallons}} of blood every day, but only about {{c2::1 to 2 quarts}} become urine.
cloze.extra: Did you know? They reabsorb most of the water and nutrients and send only waste and excess fluid to the bladder.

cloze.text: Autism spectrum disorder is a {{c1::neurodevelopmental}} disorder affecting communication, social interaction and behavior.
Autism is likely linked to genetic and environmental factors; it is {{c1::not caused by vaccines}}.
Signs of autism: difficulty with {{c1::eye contact}}, sensitivity to sound or light, {{c2::repetitive behaviors}} and delayed speech.
For patients with autism keep visits {{c1::short and predictable}} and consider {{c2::pre-visit desensitization}}.
cloze.extra: Did you know? Short, predictable visits with visual cues help.

cloze.text: For patients with autism use {{c1::quiet rooms, dim lighting}} and minimal waiting; avoid unnecessary touch or unexpected sounds.
Patients with autism may need caregiver support or {{c1::restraint}}, depending on severity.
Autism carries a high risk of bruxism, trauma, poor hygiene and {{c1::diet-related caries}} (especially if food is used as a reward).
Many patients with autism have oral sensory issues: light touch may feel irritating, while {{c1::firm pressure}} (like a lead apron) can be calming.
cloze.extra: They may struggle with gagging, bruxism or self-injury (like cheek biting).

cloze.text: Down syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by an {{c1::extra chromosome 21}}, leading to physical and intellectual delays.
Signs of Down syndrome: short stature, {{c1::flat facial profile}}, small nose, {{c2::open mouth posture}} and low muscle tone.
Down syndrome: prognathic mandible with {{c1::Class III}} malocclusion and open bite due to {{c2::tongue thrusting}}.

In Down syndrome, open-mouth posture and mouth breathing are due to {{c1::low muscle tone}} and a large tongue, and a narrowed oropharynx with enlarged tonsils and adenoids that compromise the upper airway.
Down syndrome: {{c1::fissured tongue}} and cracked lips result from mouth-breathing habits (small airways contribute to mouth breathing).
In Down syndrome, true macroglossia is rare — the tongue appears larger because the {{c1::mouth is small}}.
Down syndrome: {{c1::delayed}} exfoliation and tooth development.
Down syndrome: {{c1::microdontia}} with malformed teeth, anomalies in eruption and {{c2::congenitally missing teeth}}.
Down syndrome has a higher risk of periodontal disease due to poor oral hygiene, malocclusion, bruxism, {{c1::conical-shaped roots}} and {{c2::PMN dysfunction}}.
{{c1::Early-onset, severe periodontal disease}} is the most significant oral health issue in Down syndrome, affecting up to {{c2::90%}} of patients.
Children and young adults with Down syndrome have a {{c1::lower}} risk of dental caries because of delayed eruption, missing permanent teeth, small teeth and wider interproximal spaces.
In Down syndrome the palate may appear highly vaulted and narrow, from increased {{c1::thickness of the hard palate}}; this restricts the tongue and affects speaking and chewing.
Cleft lip and palate, as well as {{c1::bifid uvula}}, are occasionally seen in Down syndrome.
For patients with Down syndrome use {{c1::tell-show-do}}, short appointments and a calm tone, and stress caregiver involvement and home hygiene coaching.
About {{c1::40–50%}} of individuals with Down syndrome have {{c2::congenital heart defects}}; they may need premedication (consult MD).
cloze.extra: Exam standard (AHA 2021): antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated only for certain congenital heart disease — unrepaired cyanotic CHD, CHD repaired with prosthetic material (first 6 months) or with a residual defect — so consult the physician rather than premedicating every heart defect.

cloze.text: In Down syndrome, avoid neck {{c1::hyperextension}} because of {{c2::atlantoaxial instability}}.

basic.front: What does the A1C blood test measure?
basic.back: Average blood sugar over the past 2–3 months — by measuring how much glucose is attached to hemoglobin in red blood cells.

basic.front: Board Alert: why always get the A1C level of a diabetic patient?
basic.back: Whether it is below 7 or at/above 7 gives a very good indication of the periodontal status (Grade B vs C) and of how healing will happen.

basic.front: Why does diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) develop when there is no insulin (e.g., uncontrolled Type 1)?
basic.back: Without insulin glucose can't get into the cells and stays in the blood; the body thinks it's starving and burns fat for energy, releasing acidic ketones — too many ketones make the blood dangerously acidic.
basic.extra: Normally insulin lets glucose from food enter the cells to give them energy.

basic.back: Severe hypothyroidism in infants/children → stunted growth, delayed brain development and oral underdevelopment
Advanced hypothyroidism in adults → marked facial puffiness, slowed speech and bradycardia

basic.front: Why isn't HIV spread through saliva?
basic.back: Saliva contains enzymes and antibodies that break down the virus, and the amount of virus in saliva is extremely low — not nearly enough to cause infection.

typein.question: Type 1 diabetes accounts for about what percentage of diagnosed diabetes cases?
Type 2 diabetes accounts for over what percentage of diabetes cases?
Fasting blood glucose (no food for 8 hours): what value in mg/dL or more = diabetes?
typein.extra: Fasting = nothing to eat for 8 hours.

typein.question: Random blood glucose (any time, even after meals): what value in mg/dL or more, with symptoms, = diabetes?
HBV can live on surfaces for up to how many days?
typein.extra: That is why disinfection is essential even if no symptoms are present.

typein.question: AIDS is diagnosed when the CD4 count falls below what value per mm³?
Enamel hypocalcification occurs in about what percentage of persons with Down syndrome?

pairs: Delayed eruption, small jaws, crowded teeth
Macroglossia, large mandible, spacing, TMJ issues

pairs: Contaminated water; rare in North America

sort.prompt: Sort the features: Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes?
categories: May use oral meds or lifestyle changes

sort.prompt: Sort the systemic symptoms: hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism?
Sort the oral findings: hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism?
Sort the features: Addison's disease or Cushing's syndrome?

mcq.question: A patient with poorly controlled Type 1 diabetes is drowsy and has a fruity breath odor. Which condition is most likely developing?
mcq.explanation: Without insulin the body burns fat, producing acidic ketones (fruity breath) that can lead to coma = DKA. Hypoglycemia is the medication-related low-sugar emergency and has no fruity breath.

mcq.question: Which appointment plan is best for a patient with diabetes?
options: A. Long afternoon visit after lunch
B. Short morning visit with a glucose source ready
C. Late evening visit after fasting all day
D. Any time — diabetes does not affect scheduling
mcq.answer: B. Short morning visit with a glucose source ready
mcq.explanation: The book advises short, morning visits and keeping glucose ready in case of hypoglycemia (a medication side effect).

mcq.question: A patient with tremors, sweating, weight loss and a rapid pulse is scheduled for scaling with local anesthesia. Which precaution is most appropriate?
options: A. Use extra epinephrine for longer anesthesia
B. Limit epinephrine and monitor for cardiac symptoms
C. Warm the operatory because of cold intolerance
D. No special precautions are needed
mcq.answer: B. Limit epinephrine and monitor for cardiac symptoms
mcq.explanation: These are hyperthyroid signs; the book says limit epinephrine, reduce stress and watch for cardiac symptoms. Cold intolerance belongs to hypothyroidism.

mcq.question: A patient reports fatigue and low blood pressure; brown-bronze patches are seen on the buccal mucosa and gingiva. Which emergency is this patient at risk for during a stressful appointment?
mcq.explanation: Fatigue, low BP and bronze pigmentation = Addison's disease (too little cortisol); stress can trigger a life-threatening adrenal crisis. Cushing's (excess cortisol) has no crisis risk.

mcq.question: Which hepatitis virus poses the greatest risk of transmission through saliva and gingival fluid during dental care?
mcq.explanation: HBV has a moderate oral transmission risk (saliva, gingival fluid) and survives on surfaces up to 7 days. HCV is bloodborne with very low oral risk; HAV is fecal–oral with minimal oral risk.

mcq.question: A new patient has had a cough for 6 weeks with night sweats, fever and weight loss and has never been tested for TB. What is the best action?
options: A. Proceed with ultrasonic scaling using high-volume evacuation
B. Postpone non-urgent care, refer for evaluation, and notify public health if active TB is suspected
C. Treat with a surgical mask and continue
mcq.answer: B. Postpone non-urgent care, refer for evaluation, and notify public health if active TB is suspected
mcq.explanation: Possible active TB: postpone non-urgent care (N95 if seen), avoid ultrasonic/high-speed aerosols while status is unclear, and notify public health if undiagnosed active TB is suspected.

mcq.question: A 24-year-old has a painless ulcer on the lower lip that appeared about 3 weeks after a new sexual partner. Which is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Primary syphilis = painless chancre at the infection site ~3 weeks after exposure. Herpes labialis is preceded by tingling and is painful; gummas appear years later.

mcq.question: A patient arrives for a scheduled prophylaxis with an active, weeping cold sore on the lip. What should the hygienist do?
options: A. Proceed using the ultrasonic scaler
B. Reschedule the non-urgent appointment until the lesion heals
C. Proceed but avoid touching the lip
D. Proceed — recurrent lesions are not contagious
mcq.answer: B. Reschedule the non-urgent appointment until the lesion heals
mcq.explanation: HSV-1 is highly contagious in recurrent outbreaks too, with risk of herpetic whitlow, eye infection and aerosol spread; delay elective care.

mcq.question: Which group of oral findings should the hygienist expect to monitor in a patient with end-stage renal disease?
options: A. Bronze gingival pigmentation and early eruption
B. Uremic breath, metallic taste, xerostomia and bleeding gingiva
D. Painless chancre and mucous patches
mcq.answer: B. Uremic breath, metallic taste, xerostomia and bleeding gingiva
mcq.explanation: The book lists uremic breath, metallic taste, xerostomia, candidiasis, stomatitis and bleeding gingiva for ESRD. Bronze pigmentation = Addison's; macroglossia/delayed eruption = hypothyroidism.

mcq.question: Which approach is most appropriate for a child with autism spectrum disorder who is sensitive to sound and touch?
options: A. Long appointment in a busy open-bay clinic
B. Short, predictable visit in a quiet, dimly lit room, with firm pressure such as a lead apron
C. Frequent light touches to build trust
D. Surprise the patient with new instruments each visit
mcq.answer: B. Short, predictable visit in a quiet, dimly lit room, with firm pressure such as a lead apron
mcq.explanation: The book: short, predictable visits, quiet rooms, dim lighting, minimal waiting; light touch can irritate while firm pressure (lead apron) can calm.

mcq.question: What is the most significant oral health issue in patients with Down syndrome?
mcq.explanation: Up to 90% are affected by early-onset severe periodontal disease (PMN dysfunction, conical roots, poor hygiene). Caries risk is actually LOWER in children/young adults; hypocalcification ~20%; clefts only occasional.

mcq.question: While positioning a patient with Down syndrome, the hygienist should avoid which movement, and why?
options: A. Reclining the chair — risk of syncope
C. Turning the head to the side — macroglossia
mcq.explanation: Atlantoaxial instability makes neck hyperextension dangerous in Down syndrome.

mcq.question: Which condition is most likely to cause gingival hyperplasia due to an anti-rejection medication?
mcq.explanation: Patients with ESRD often receive kidney transplants. To prevent organ rejection they are prescribed cyclosporine (Sandimmune), which commonly causes gingival hyperplasia.

mcq.question: A patient presents with exophthalmos, weight loss, and rapid heart rate. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Exophthalmos (bulging eyes), tachycardia and weight loss are classic signs of Graves' disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.

mcq.question: Which type of stroke occurs due to a blood vessel rupture?
mcq.explanation: A hemorrhagic stroke is caused by bleeding into the brain when a blood vessel ruptures, leading to increased pressure and damage.

mcq.question: Why is brushing immediately after vomiting discouraged in patients with bulimia?
options: C. It pushes acid deeper into enamel
D. It leads to gingival recession
mcq.answer: C. It pushes acid deeper into enamel
mcq.explanation: After vomiting, enamel is softened by stomach acid. Brushing too soon can abrade the weakened enamel, worsening erosion. A neutral rinse should be used first.

mcq.question: What is the role of A1C in diabetes management?
options: C. Reflects average blood sugar over 2–3 months
D. Measures blood sugar after fasting
mcq.answer: C. Reflects average blood sugar over 2–3 months
mcq.explanation: A1C measures the percentage of hemoglobin coated with sugar, reflecting long-term glucose control — key for managing diabetes.

mcq.question: Which correctly describes systolic and diastolic blood pressure?
options: A. Diastolic pressure is higher than systolic pressure in a normal reading.
B. Systolic pressure measures pressure during heart relaxation; diastolic during contraction.
C. Both systolic and diastolic occur when the heart is resting.
D. Systolic pressure occurs during heart contraction; diastolic pressure occurs when the heart relaxes.
mcq.answer: D. Systolic pressure occurs during heart contraction; diastolic pressure occurs when the heart relaxes.
mcq.explanation: This describes the cardiac cycle: systolic is the peak pressure during left ventricular contraction, and diastolic is the lowest pressure during relaxation.

mcq.question: A 65-year-old patient in your dental chair suddenly develops slurred speech, facial drooping on one side, and inability to raise one arm fully. What is the most likely medical emergency occurring?
mcq.explanation: Facial droop, arm weakness and slurred speech are hallmark signs of a stroke (useful acronym: F.A.S.T. — Face, Arm, Speech, Time).

mcq.question: Which features help differentiate stable angina from myocardial infarction during a dental appointment?
options: A. Angina pain usually lasts longer than 30 minutes and radiates to the left arm.
B. Angina is not relieved by nitroglycerin, while myocardial infarction is.
C. Stable angina typically resolves with rest or nitroglycerin within 5–10 minutes.
D. Myocardial infarction presents with sharp, localized chest pain relieved by deep breathing.
mcq.answer: C. Stable angina typically resolves with rest or nitroglycerin within 5–10 minutes.
mcq.explanation: Stable angina is predictable, triggered by exertion or stress, and typically resolves within 5–10 minutes with rest or nitroglycerin.

mcq.question: A patient with an INR of 3.8 is scheduled for a dental extraction. What should the clinician do FIRST?
options: A. Proceed as planned with extra gauze
B. Contact the patient's physician for medical clearance
C. Cancel the procedure and refer to ER
D. Prescribe aspirin to reduce inflammation
mcq.answer: B. Contact the patient's physician for medical clearance
mcq.explanation: An INR >3.5 indicates high bleeding risk (e.g., warfarin). Elective procedures should be delayed, and a medical consult is recommended to evaluate safety.

mcq.question: Which of the following oral signs is most likely seen in a patient with untreated HIV/AIDS and CD4 count <200/mm³?
options: C. Hairy leukoplakia on the tongue
mcq.answer: C. Hairy leukoplakia on the tongue
mcq.explanation: Hairy leukoplakia is a common opportunistic infection seen in immunocompromised patients and appears as white patches on the lateral tongue.

mcq.question: Which blood disorder is characterized by normal platelets but a defective clotting cascade, leading to weak fibrin formation?
mcq.explanation: Hemophilia is a genetic disorder in which clotting factors (like VIII or IX) are missing, so the platelet plug forms but no stable fibrin clot develops.

mcq.question: A patient with spina bifida should be asked about which specific allergy before treatment?
mcq.explanation: Patients with spina bifida have a high risk of developing latex allergy due to repeated surgeries and exposure to latex products from early life.

mcq.question: A patient on dialysis is best scheduled for dental care:
mcq.explanation: Dialysis can lead to temporary anticoagulation and fatigue. The day after allows for hemodynamic stabilization and lowers bleeding risk.

mcq.question: Which of the following symptoms is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?
mcq.explanation: Parkinson's affects the dopamine-producing neurons in the brain (basal ganglia), leading to a tremor at rest, slow movements (bradykinesia) and rigidity.

mcq.question: Which endocrine disorder leads to delayed tooth eruption, macroglossia, and mental retardation if not treated early?
mcq.explanation: Cretinism is untreated hypothyroidism in children and severely affects mental and physical development, including oral growth.
